181.quote_or_event: “For eight causes discipline is called virtue, viz.: not to be fond of mirth, to control one's self, not to speak evil of others, not to be without discipline, not to be of wrong discipline, not to be covetous, not to be choleric, to love the truth; for their influence discipline is called virtue.”
181.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana names refraining from speaking evil of others as one of the eight marks that make a monk's discipline count as virtue.
181.tie_back: Valluvar grants that a man who does nothing else right still earns one good word for not backbiting, and the Jain text likewise counts not speaking evil of others as a virtue in its own right.
181._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good thematic fit, though the Jain list is about a monk's discipline and lacks the Kural's ironic concession about a man who is otherwise without virtue.

182.quote_or_event: “पिट्ठिमंसं न खाएज्जा” (piṭṭhimaṃsaṃ na khāejjā) — “One should not talk ill of others in their absence.”
182.explanation: The Daśavaikālika forbids a monk to 'eat the flesh of the back', its idiom for running people down when they are not there, and the tradition treats such talk as cowardly.
182.tie_back: Valluvar says tearing a man down behind his back and smiling at his face is worse than open wrongdoing, and the Jain sūtra uses the same 'behind the back' image to ban that kind of talk outright.
182.source: Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.47, Prakrit line with English rendering as given on tattvagyan.com ('Do not talk ill behind someone's back')
182._accuracy_note: Prakrit line and English rendering verified verbatim on tattvagyan.com (a long-running Jain devotional site, web tier, not checked against a printed translation); a very close fit for backbiting, but it does not cover the Kural's point about the false smile to the face.

183.quote_or_event: “Indifferent and pure with regard to every kind of control, a Śramaṇa should walk about; he who entertains pure thoughts during his whole life, dies as a worthy and wise man.”
183.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga holds that a life kept pure in thought ends in a worthy death, so the quality of a death depends on how the life was lived.
183.tie_back: Valluvar says death is better than a life kept going by backbiting and falsehood, and the Jain verse likewise judges a life by whether it can end in a pure and worthy death.
183._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match only, since the verse speaks of pure conduct and a worthy death in general and says nothing about backbiting or about death being better than a dishonest life.

184.quote_or_event: “If our intention is to remove the fault of a man, then we should tell his faults in his presence only so that he can reflect on them and eliminate the same. To tell someone's mistake in his presence is an act of bravery; but we should take care to tell him or her in privacy.”
184.explanation: Explaining the Daśavaikālika's ban on talking ill of people in their absence, this Jain gloss says a fault should be named to the person's face, privately and kindly, and never behind their back.
184.tie_back: Valluvar allows even harsh words spoken to a man's face but never thoughtless words behind his back, and the Jain gloss draws the same line between correcting someone to their face and talking about them when they are absent.
184.source: Modern explanatory gloss on Daśavaikālika Sūtra 8.47, tattvagyan.com ('Do not talk ill behind someone's back')
184._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on tattvagyan.com, but these words are the site's modern commentary on the sūtra, not scripture; it is close to the Kural's face-versus-back contrast, though the Jain gloss asks for gentle private correction rather than accepting harsh speech.

185.quote_or_event: “Censuring others, praising oneself, concealing good qualities present in others and proclaiming noble qualities absent in oneself, cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas which lead to low-status (nīcagotra).”
185.explanation: Umāsvāti puts running others down and claiming virtues one does not have side by side as causes of karma that leads to rebirth in low status.
185.tie_back: Valluvar says a man's backbiting shows that his talk of virtue is hollow, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra pairs that same censure of others with the false display of virtues one does not have.
185.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.25 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
185._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; a strong fit, since both texts link censuring others with a false claim to virtue, though the sūtra frames it as karmic cause rather than as evidence of a hollow heart.

186.quote_or_event: “A man who insults another will long whirl in the Circle of Births; to blame others is not good. Considering this a sage is not conceited.”
186.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga warns that insulting and blaming others binds karma that keeps the insulter in the cycle of rebirth for a long time.
186.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who spreads others' faults will have his own worst faults spread in turn, and the Jain text likewise says blaming others comes back on the one who blames, here as long bondage to rebirth.
186._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; both texts say blaming others recoils on the blamer, but the Kural's recoil is social (others expose your faults) while the Jain one is karmic.

187.quote_or_event: “A monk or a nun, well considering, should not use speech whether truth or untruth, or truth mixed with untruth, if it be sinful, blamable, rough, stinging, coarse, hard, leading to sins, to discord and factions, to grief and outrage, to destruction of living beings.”
187.explanation: The Ācārāṅga forbids any speech, even true speech, that leads to discord and factions or causes grief.
187.tie_back: Valluvar condemns words that split people apart and drive away even close friends, and the Ācārāṅga bans speech that leads to discord and factions even when what it says is true.
187.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.4.1.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
187._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a clear fit for speech that divides, though the rule is a general monastic rule on speech and does not single out talk behind people's backs.

188.quote_or_event: “If he is frequently angry; if he perseveres in his wrath; if he spurns friendly advice; if he is proud of his learning; if he finds fault with others; if he is angry even with friends; if he speaks evil even of a good friend behind his back; ... then he is called ill-behaved.”
188.explanation: Among the fourteen faults that mark an ill-behaved monk who cannot reach nirvāṇa, the Uttarādhyayana lists speaking evil even of a good friend behind his back.
188.tie_back: Valluvar asks what a man who spreads the faults even of those closest to him would not do to strangers, and the Jain text singles out exactly this, slandering even a good friend behind his back, as a sign of bad character.
188._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (the ellipsis leaves out the rest of the list); a close fit for backbiting against intimates, though it lacks the Kural's argument from friends to strangers.

189.quote_or_event: “Though life cannot be prolonged, as the saying is, still foolish people sin recklessly; a foolish man is filled to the brim (as it were) with sins. Considering this a sage is not conceited.”
189.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga pictures the reckless fool as a vessel filled to the brim with sin, a heavy load of karma he has made for himself.
189.tie_back: Valluvar wonders whether the earth bears the slanderer's weight only out of duty, and the Jain verse likewise pictures the reckless sinner as loaded to the brim with sin.
189._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a weak next-best match, since the verse is about reckless sin in general and has neither the slanderer nor the Kural's image of the patient earth.

190.quote_or_event: “The opposites of those mentioned in the previous sūtra and humility (namravṛtti) and modesty (anutseka) cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas that lead to high-status (uccagotra).”
190.explanation: Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi, given with the sūtra, explains the opposites as censuring oneself, praising others, proclaiming the real qualities of others and not claiming qualities one lacks.
190.tie_back: Valluvar asks what harm could come if people saw their own faults as clearly as others' faults, and the Tattvārtha Sūtra praises exactly that reversal: blaming oneself instead of others.
190.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.26, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
190._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; the fit depends on the commentary's gloss (self-censure, praise of others) rather than the bare sūtra, and the Jain reward is karmic status rather than the Kural's end of harm to living beings.
